reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: Caused by a postzygotic activating variant in AKT1, resulting in somatic mosaicism, so the condition is sporadic and non-inherited
Defined by progressive, asymmetric and disproportionate overgrowth of bone, connective tissue, skin and other tissues that worsens over childhood
The cerebriform connective tissue naevus, most often on the soles, is a highly specific hallmark
Overgrowth is characteristically distorting and mosaic in distribution, sparing some areas while dramatically affecting others
Associated features include vascular malformations, lipomatous overgrowth or regional lipohypoplasia, and epidermal naevi
There is a significant risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, a major cause of premature death, warranting heightened perioperative vigilance
The AKT1 variant activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth-signalling pathway, driving the tissue overgrowth
reference.pathophysiology: Proteus syndrome is caused by a specific activating variant in AKT1 arising after fertilisation, producing a mosaic population of cells carrying the change; a constitutional (germline) variant is thought to be lethal, which is why the disorder occurs only as somatic mosaicism. AKT1 is a central kinase in the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mTOR signalling pathway, and constitutive activation promotes cell growth, proliferation and survival. Because only a subset of cells is affected and this expands during development, the result is progressive, patchy and disproportionate overgrowth of the involved tissues. The variable tissue distribution accounts for the striking clinical heterogeneity.
additionalDifferentials: PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS), including CLOVES syndrome
Maffucci syndrome and other vascular/skeletal overgrowth conditions
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for the AKT1 activating variant on affected (lesional) tissue given mosaicism
Skeletal imaging to assess progressive bony overgrowth and deformity
MRI to characterise soft-tissue, lipomatous and vascular components
Vascular imaging and Doppler studies for malformations and thrombosis risk
Histopathology of the cerebriform connective tissue naevus or other lesions
Assessment for pulmonary cystic disease and abdominal/pelvic tumours where indicated
redFlags: Symptoms or signs of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, especially perioperatively
Rapidly progressive overgrowth causing functional impairment or airway/organ compromise
Neurological symptoms from central nervous system or skull involvement
New masses raising concern for the tumours occasionally associated with the syndrome
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely with the extent and location of overgrowth; progressive skeletal deformity and functional disability are common, and venous thromboembolism is a leading cause of premature mortality. Multidisciplinary management can reduce complications, but the overgrowth itself is difficult to reverse.
pitfalls: Testing unaffected blood and missing the low-level mosaic AKT1 variant present only in lesional tissue
Applying the label loosely to any overgrowth condition rather than meeting stringent diagnostic criteria
Underestimating thromboembolic risk around surgery and immobilisation
Confusing the condition with PIK3CA-related overgrowth, which has different management implications
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Address the markedly raised risk of venous thromboembolism with vigilant thromboprophylaxis, especially perioperatively, as pulmonary embolism is a leading cause of premature death
Manage progressive skeletal overgrowth and deformity with orthopaedic surgery, epiphysiodesis and orthotics to preserve function
Consider AKT-pathway targeted therapy such as the AKT inhibitor miransertib, currently within trials, given the underlying AKT1 and PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation
Treat vascular malformations and lipomatous overgrowth with appropriate surgical, interventional or debulking procedures
Undertake surveillance for complications including pulmonary cystic disease and abdominal or pelvic tumours
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across orthopaedics, plastic surgery, dermatology, vascular and respiratory specialties
Provide genetic counselling explaining the postzygotic mosaic AKT1 cause, reassuring that the condition is sporadic and not inherited
